key_insight: Storage capacity of a d×d linear associative memory is controlled not just by matrix degrees of freedom but by the retrieval rule: top-1 (winner-take-all) retrieval requires a larger memory scale (d^2 ≍ n log n) than coarser / listwise criteria, producing sharp capacity thresholds.
problem_solved: Determines how many key–value pairs a linear memory can reliably store and retrieve, and shows that achievable capacity fundamentally depends on the retrieval criterion (top-1 vs listwise) rather than only on parameter count.
method: Analyze an isotropic Gaussian model of stored key–value pairs to obtain probabilistic capacity bounds.
Study the correlation-matrix (superposition) memory construction and derive sharp thresholds for successful retrieval under different criteria.
Combine probabilistic/threshold analysis to contrast winner-take-all (top-1) and listwise retrieval regimes.
impact: Clarifies fundamental trade-offs between memory size and retrieval requirements, guiding design of associative memory layers and retrieval mechanisms in neural architectures; tells practitioners when extra capacity (≈log n factor) is necessary for exact top-1 recall.
visual_elements: Phase-transition plot: probability of successful retrieval vs normalized memory size (d^2/n) showing sharp thresholds for top-1 and listwise regimes.
Side-by-side schematics: winner-take-all (top-1) retrieval vs listwise retrieval highlighting different failure modes (largest distractor vs average confusion).
Illustration of correlation-matrix superposition: how multiple key–value pairs are stored and cause interference.
Compact table or icon row comparing required scaling: top-1 (d^2 ≍ n log n) vs weaker retrieval (lower scaling).
paper_title: Sharp Capacity Thresholds in Linear Associative Memory: From Winner-Take-All to Listwise Retrieval
paper_authors: Nicholas Barnfield, Juno Kim, Eshaan Nichani, Jason D. Lee, Yue M. Lu
